Required Packages

library(NNS)
library(prophet)
packageVersion("NNS")
## [1] '13.3'
packageVersion("prophet")
## [1] '1.1.7'

Comparison Design

Each comparison gives both methods the same training data and forecast origin and scores the same horizon. Neither method is tuned on the test window: prophet runs with its default settings, and NNS.ARMA uses either calendar lags fixed in advance or the periods NNS.seas finds in the training data. A last-value forecast is scored alongside as a reference.

The archived page (November 2017) differed in three ways. It chose the Peyton Manning periods with the lowest error on the test year, which made that year part of the tuning; its lynx prophet forecast had 35 values for 34 test years; and its S&P 500 data came from Yahoo Finance, which this build cannot download. Its scores and tallies are not carried forward.

rmse <- function(f, a) sqrt(mean((f - a)^2))
# Download a file once per build and check it is the version this page used.
fetch <- function(url, md5) {
  path <- file.path(tempdir(), basename(url))
  if (!file.exists(path)) download.file(url, path, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
  stopifnot(unname(tools::md5sum(path)) == md5)
  path
}
results <- list()
record <- function(name, h, prophet_fc, nns_fc, actual, last_value, seconds) {
  results[[name]] <<- data.frame(Comparison = name, Horizon = h,
                                 `prophet RMSE` = rmse(prophet_fc, actual),
                                 `NNS RMSE` = rmse(nns_fc, actual),
                                 `Last value RMSE` = rmse(last_value, actual),
                                 `prophet s` = seconds[1], `NNS s` = seconds[2],
                                 check.names = FALSE)
  results[[name]][, 3:5]
}
timed <- function(expr) {
  t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
  value <- expr
  list(value = value, seconds = proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0)
}

Retail Sales Example

Below is the retail sales data incorporated with the Facebook prophet repository.

retail <- read.csv(fetch(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/facebook/prophet/main/examples/example_retail_sales.csv",
  "efbd7c178abf498e5db39eb1ff3c84a3"))
retail$ds <- as.Date(retail$ds)
range(retail$ds)
## [1] "1992-01-01" "2016-05-01"

We are forecasting the last 50 periods…

l <- length(retail[, 1]) - 50

prophet model:

p <- timed({
  m <- prophet(retail[1:l, ])
  predict(m, data.frame(ds = retail$ds[(l + 1):nrow(retail)]))
})
## Disabling weekly seasonality. Run prophet with weekly.seasonality=TRUE to override this.
## Disabling daily seasonality. Run prophet with daily.seasonality=TRUE to override this.
retail_fcst <- p$value
plot(m, predict(m, data.frame(ds = retail$ds)))

NNS model:

NNS uses the 12-month calendar lag and a linear regression of each lag’s components.

n <- timed(NNS.ARMA(retail[, 2], h = 50, seasonal.factor = 12, method = 'lin',
                    training.set = l, seasonal.plot = FALSE))

nns.retail.fcst <- n$value

MSE:

c(prophet = mean((retail_fcst$yhat - tail(retail[, 2], 50))^2),
  NNS = mean((nns.retail.fcst - tail(retail[, 2], 50))^2))
##    prophet        NNS 
## 2369088008   52793721
record("Retail sales", 50, retail_fcst$yhat, nns.retail.fcst, tail(retail[, 2], 50),
       retail[l, 2], c(p$seconds, n$seconds))
##   prophet RMSE NNS RMSE Last value RMSE
## 1     48673.28 7265.929        34167.38

Peyton Manning Example (Raw Values)

Next is the Peyton Manning example from the Facebook prophet repository: daily log page views of Peyton Manning’s Wikipedia page. The repository now ships only the log file; the raw views are its exponent. Twenty-nine days are missing, so NNS.ARMA’s lags count observations rather than calendar days, while prophet uses the dates.

log_omaha <- read.csv(fetch(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/facebook/prophet/main/examples/example_wp_log_peyton_manning.csv",
  "43a15e3f903a6e82cc0a53f0be249575"))
log_omaha$ds <- as.Date(log_omaha$ds)
omaha <- data.frame(ds = log_omaha$ds, y = exp(log_omaha$y))
range(omaha$ds)
## [1] "2007-12-10" "2016-01-20"
sum(diff(omaha$ds) > 1)
## [1] 29

We are forecasting the last 365 periods…

l <- length(omaha[, 1]) - 365
test_days <- omaha$ds[(l + 1):nrow(omaha)]

prophet model:

p <- timed({
  m <- prophet(omaha[1:l, ])
  predict(m, data.frame(ds = test_days))
})
## Disabling daily seasonality. Run prophet with daily.seasonality=TRUE to override this.
omaha_fcst <- p$value
plot(m, predict(m, data.frame(ds = omaha$ds)))

NNS model:

NNS is using a seasonal.factor = c(1, sf), which translates to a daily and the best reported lag from our seasonality test on the training data. This is not optimized.

sf <- NNS.seas(omaha[1:l, 2], plot = FALSE)$best.period
sf
## [1] 362
n <- timed(NNS.ARMA(omaha[, 2], h = 365, seasonal.factor = c(1, sf), method = 'lin',
                    training.set = l, seasonal.plot = FALSE))

nns.omaha.fcst <- n$value

MSE:

c(prophet = mean((omaha_fcst$yhat - tail(omaha[, 2], 365))^2),
  NNS = mean((nns.omaha.fcst - tail(omaha[, 2], 365))^2))
##   prophet       NNS 
## 137562729 153994867
record("Peyton Manning, raw", 365, omaha_fcst$yhat, nns.omaha.fcst, tail(omaha[, 2], 365),
       omaha[l, 2], c(p$seconds, n$seconds))
##   prophet RMSE NNS RMSE Last value RMSE
## 1     11728.71 12409.47        11938.17

Peyton Manning Example (Log Values)

Using the log values of the preceding Peyton Manning dataset. Again, we are forecasting the last 365 periods…

prophet model:

p <- timed({
  m <- prophet(log_omaha[1:l, ])
  predict(m, data.frame(ds = test_days))
})
## Disabling daily seasonality. Run prophet with daily.seasonality=TRUE to override this.
log_omaha_fcst <- p$value
plot(m, predict(m, data.frame(ds = log_omaha$ds)))

NNS model:

sf <- NNS.seas(log_omaha[1:l, 2], plot = FALSE)$best.period
sf
## [1] 362
n <- timed(NNS.ARMA(log_omaha[, 2], h = 365, seasonal.factor = c(1, sf), method = 'nonlin',
                    training.set = l, seasonal.plot = FALSE))

nns.log.omaha.fcst <- n$value

MSE:

c(prophet = mean((log_omaha_fcst$yhat - tail(log_omaha[, 2], 365))^2),
  NNS = mean((nns.log.omaha.fcst - tail(log_omaha[, 2], 365))^2))
##   prophet       NNS 
## 0.2874548 0.5636633
record("Peyton Manning, log", 365, log_omaha_fcst$yhat, nns.log.omaha.fcst,
       tail(log_omaha[, 2], 365), log_omaha[l, 2], c(p$seconds, n$seconds))
##   prophet RMSE  NNS RMSE Last value RMSE
## 1    0.5361481 0.7507751        1.365399

Notes

Can we recover better raw estimates from translated log estimates for prophet, or better log estimates from translated raw estimates for NNS? The exponent of a log forecast is a median-type forecast of the raw views, not their mean.

c(`prophet, exp(log forecast) vs raw` = mean((exp(log_omaha_fcst$yhat) - tail(omaha[, 2], 365))^2),
  `prophet, raw forecast vs raw` = mean((omaha_fcst$yhat - tail(omaha[, 2], 365))^2))
## prophet, exp(log forecast) vs raw      prophet, raw forecast vs raw 
##                         121964956                         137562729
c(`NNS, log(raw forecast) vs log` = mean((log(nns.omaha.fcst) - tail(log_omaha[, 2], 365))^2),
  `NNS, log forecast vs log` = mean((nns.log.omaha.fcst - tail(log_omaha[, 2], 365))^2))
## NNS, log(raw forecast) vs log      NNS, log forecast vs log 
##                     2.2861224                     0.5636633

lynx Dataset

Next we test the Canadian lynx dataset suggested from Andrew Gelman’s blog post on prophet: http://andrewgelman.com/2017/03/01/facebooks-prophet-uses-stan/. The annual trappings from 1821 to 1934 are split into the first 80 years for training and the last 34 for testing.

data(lynx)
l <- length(lynx) - 34
lynx_df <- data.frame(ds = as.Date(paste0(time(lynx), "-01-01")), y = as.numeric(lynx))

prophet model and RMSE:

p <- timed({
  m <- prophet(lynx_df[1:l, ])
  predict(m, data.frame(ds = lynx_df$ds[(l + 1):nrow(lynx_df)]))
})
## Disabling weekly seasonality. Run prophet with weekly.seasonality=TRUE to override this.
## Disabling daily seasonality. Run prophet with daily.seasonality=TRUE to override this.
fcast <- p$value
sqrt(mean((tail(lynx, 34) - fcast$yhat)^2))
## [1] 1965.652
plot(m, predict(m, data.frame(ds = lynx_df$ds)))

NNS model and RMSE:

NNS uses the two best periods NNS.seas finds in the 80 training years.

n <- timed(NNS.ARMA(lynx, h = 34, training.set = l, method = 'lin', seasonal.factor = FALSE,
                    best.periods = 2, seasonal.plot = FALSE))

nns.lynx <- n$value
sqrt(mean((nns.lynx - tail(lynx, 34))^2))
## [1] 1433.139
record("lynx", 34, fcast$yhat, nns.lynx, tail(lynx, 34), lynx[l], c(p$seconds, n$seconds))
##   prophet RMSE NNS RMSE Last value RMSE
## 1     1965.652 1433.139        2338.895

S&P 500

Finally we are going to forecast 252 trading days of the S&P 500 index, at three consecutive forecast origins. The archived page used SPY prices from 2007 to 2017 downloaded from Yahoo Finance with quantmod. This build uses FRED’s SP500 series (index closes from S&P Dow Jones Indices), downloaded at build time; FRED keeps the most recent ten years. Each origin is trained on the 1260 trading days (about five years) before it, so the windows stay inside FRED’s range when the page is rebuilt, until late 2028.

sp <- read.csv("https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=SP500", na.strings = ".")
sp <- sp[!is.na(sp[[2]]), ]
sp <- data.frame(ds = as.Date(sp[[1]]), y = sp[[2]])
sp <- sp[sp$ds <= as.Date("2026-10-30"), ]
origins <- nrow(sp) - 252 * (3:1)
data.frame(Year = 1:3,
           `Training from` = sp$ds[origins - 1259], `Origin` = sp$ds[origins],
           `Test from` = sp$ds[origins + 1], `Test to` = sp$ds[origins + 252],
           check.names = FALSE)
##   Year Training from     Origin  Test from    Test to
## 1    1    2018-10-23 2023-10-25 2023-10-26 2024-10-25
## 2    2    2019-10-24 2024-10-25 2024-10-28 2025-10-29
## 3    3    2020-10-23 2025-10-29 2025-10-30 2026-10-30

NNS is using a seasonal.factor = c(1, 5, 21, 63, 126, 252), which translates to a daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly, bi-annual and annual lag for S&P closing prices.

par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (k in 1:3) {
  window <- (origins[k] - 1259):(origins[k] + 252)
  train <- sp[window[1:1260], ]
  test <- sp[window[1261:1512], ]
  p <- timed({
    m <- prophet(train)
    predict(m, data.frame(ds = test$ds))
  })
  n <- timed(NNS.ARMA(train$y, h = 252, seasonal.factor = c(1, 5, 21, 63, 126, 252),
                      method = 'nonlin', plot = FALSE, seasonal.plot = FALSE))
  print(record(paste0("S&P 500, year ", k), 252, p$value$yhat, n$value, test$y,
               tail(train$y, 1), c(p$seconds, n$seconds)))
  plot(c(train$ds, test$ds), c(train$y, test$y), type = "l", xlab = "", ylab = "S&P 500",
       main = paste0("Year ", k, ": ", test$ds[1], " to ", test$ds[252]))
  lines(test$ds, p$value$yhat, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
  lines(test$ds, n$value, col = "red", lwd = 2)
  abline(v = train$ds[1260], lty = 3)
  legend("topleft", legend = c("Actual", "prophet", "NNS"), col = c("black", "blue", "red"),
         lty = 1, lwd = c(1, 2, 2), bty = "n")
}
## Disabling daily seasonality. Run prophet with daily.seasonality=TRUE to override this.
##   prophet RMSE NNS RMSE Last value RMSE
## 1     432.4406 802.5419        1069.047
## Disabling daily seasonality. Run prophet with daily.seasonality=TRUE to override this.
##   prophet RMSE NNS RMSE Last value RMSE
## 1     581.0286 318.1865        461.1854
## Disabling daily seasonality. Run prophet with daily.seasonality=TRUE to override this.
##   prophet RMSE NNS RMSE Last value RMSE
## 1     334.0668 336.5259        512.4236

Summary

summary_table <- do.call(rbind, results)
knitr::kable(summary_table, digits = c(0, 0, 4, 4, 4, 1, 1), row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Test RMSE and run time (seconds) of each forecast")
Test RMSE and run time (seconds) of each forecast
Comparison Horizon prophet RMSE NNS RMSE Last value RMSE prophet s NNS s
Retail sales 50 48673.2782 7265.9288 34167.3821 1.8 0.0
Peyton Manning, raw 365 11728.7139 12409.4668 11938.1719 2.0 0.1
Peyton Manning, log 365 0.5361 0.7508 1.3654 1.6 3.6
lynx 34 1965.6522 1433.1391 2338.8946 0.6 0.0
S&P 500, year 1 252 432.4406 802.5419 1069.0471 1.5 3.0
S&P 500, year 2 252 581.0286 318.1865 461.1854 1.5 3.1
S&P 500, year 3 252 334.0668 336.5259 512.4236 1.3 2.9

NNS.ARMA has the lower RMSE in 3 of these 7 forecasts and prophet in 4. The last-value forecast is more accurate than prophet in 2 and than NNS.ARMA in 1. Each prophet fit took 0.6 to 2.0 seconds here and each NNS.ARMA forecast 0.0 to 3.6 seconds.

These are single forecast origins for retail sales, Peyton Manning (raw and log) and lynx, and three consecutive years of the S&P 500, so they describe these windows rather than rank the methods. A ranking would need many origins per series, scored with the same data, origins, horizon and tuning budget for every method.

To be fair, prophet was not altered from its default settings and any interested readers are more than welcome to suggest different settings to improve performance. NNS was not optimized either.

Note (2026). The archived page’s scores, including the running tally, came from test-window period selection (Peyton Manning), a misaligned lynx comparison and SPY data that cannot be reproduced; they are withdrawn. See examples/example-corrections.md.
